en: Thus have I heard: Dīgha Nikāya 10 Subhasutta Thus have I heard: [the Blessed One was once staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. Then the brahmin Subha, Todeyya’s son, approached the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side and said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, it is said: ‘The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, anything else is worthless. And it is said: ‘The world is not eternal; this alone is the truth, anything else is worthless. … ‘The world is finite… infinite… the soul and the body are the same… the soul is one thing and the body another… after death a Tathāgata exists… does not exist… both exists and does not exist… neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is the truth, anything else is worthless. Now, Master Gotama, what is the true fact here? What is the actual state of affairs? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, as to those who say: ‘The world is eternal; this alone is the truth, anything else is worthless’—this is their view. As to those who say: ‘The world is not eternal…’ … ‘after death a Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is the truth, anything else is worthless’—this is their view. Subha, when one has seen well with right wisdom how these things arise, it is impossible that one would say: ‘The world is eternal… neither exists nor does not exist; this alone is the truth, anything else is worthless. [Subha asked:

“But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘Beyond this there is nothing more’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘Beyond this there is nothing more. But, Subha, there are four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? There is the case where a certain person is a body-witness (kāyasakkhin), one who has attained to the realization of the ultimate goal of the holy life in this very life, having directly experienced it with superior wisdom, and dwells therein. There is the case where a certain person is one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta), who has gained confidence in the Dhamma through his own experience of the teachings. There is the case where a certain person is one liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta), who has reached the destruction of the taints through wisdom. And there is the case where a certain person is a faith-follower (saddhānusārī), one who follows the Dhamma out of faith. These, Subha, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘This is the final birth, there is no more becoming’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘This is the final birth, there is no more becoming. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I am the one who knows and sees’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I am the one who knows and sees. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I neither know nor see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I neither know nor see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I will know, I will see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I will know, I will see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I might know, I might see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I might know, I might see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see, but I will not know, I will not see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see, but I will not know, I will not see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see, and whether there is something beyond or not, I do not know, I do not see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see, and whether there is something beyond or not, I do not know, I do not see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I know, I see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I know, I see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I neither know nor see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I neither know nor see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I will know, I will see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I will know, I will see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world.

[Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I might know, I might see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I might know, I might see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see, but I will not know, I will not see’? [The Blessed One replied: “Subha, there is no ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus: ‘I do not know, I do not see, but I will not know, I will not see. But, Subha, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. [Subha asked: “But, Master Gotama, is there any ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees thus
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park, not long after the Blessed One had attained final Nibbāna.
Now at that time the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, was residing at Sāvatthī for some business or other.
Then the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, addressed a certain young brahmin:

“Come, young man, go to where the ascetic Ānanda is; having approached him, in my name ask the ascetic Ānanda whether he is free from illness, free from affliction, light in body, strong, and dwelling in comfort:
‘The young man Subha, son of Todeyya, asks whether the venerable Ānanda is free from illness, free from affliction, light in body, strong, and dwelling in comfort.
And speak thus:”
“It would be well, indeed, if the venerable Ānanda would visit the residence of the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, out of compassion.
“Yes, sir,” that young brahmin replied to Subha, the son of Todeyya. He then approached the Venerable Ānanda and exchanged greetings with him.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the young brahmin said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“The young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, asks after the venerable Ānanda’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, strength, and well-being;
and he says this:
‘It would be well, indeed, if the venerable Ānanda would visit the residence of the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, out of compassion.’”
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to that young man:
"It is not the right time, young man.
I have drunk a dose of medicine today."
“Perhaps we might also go to him ourselves, taking the right time and the right occasion.

“Very well, sir,” that young brahmin replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Rising from his seat, he approached the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, and having approached him, he said this to the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya:
“We have already spoken to the venerable Ānanda on your behalf.”
“The young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, asks after the venerable Ānanda’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, strength, and well-being, and he says this:
‘It would be good, indeed, if the venerable Ānanda would visit the residence of the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, out of compassion.
When this was said, sir, the ascetic Ānanda said this to me:”
“It is not the right time, young brahmin.
I have drunk a dose of medicine today.
Perhaps we might visit you tomorrow, taking into account the proper time and occasion.”
"To this extent, sir, it is already enough; for the venerable Ānanda has granted me the opportunity to come at a later time.

Then, when that night had passed, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and with the bhikkhu Cetaka as his attendant, went to the residence of the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya.
He approached him; having approached, he sat down on the prepared seat. Then the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, approached the Venerable Ānanda;
having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the young brahmin Subha, the son of Todeyya, said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Master Ānanda has long been the attendant of the venerable Gotama, living in his presence and moving about near him.
Master Ānanda would surely know those teachings of which the venerable Gotama was a proponent, and wherein he exhorted, settled, and established this generation.
Of what teachings, Master Ānanda, was the venerable Gotama a proponent; and wherein did he exhort, settle, and establish this generation?”
“Māṇava, that Blessed One was a speaker in praise of three aggregates; therein he incited, settled, and established this generation. Which three?
The noble aggregate of virtue, the noble aggregate of concentration, and the noble aggregate of wisdom.”
“Māṇava, it was of these three aggregates that the Blessed One spoke in praise; therein he incited, settled, and established this generation.
“But what, Master Ānanda, is that noble aggregate of virtue which the venerable Gotama spoke in praise of, wherein he incited, settled, and established this generation?”

“Here, student, a Tathāgata arises in the world, an arahant, perfectly enlightened, endowed with knowledge and conduct, well-gone, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Having realized this world—with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans—by his own direct knowledge, he makes it known.”
He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals the holy life, entirely complete and pure.
A householder, or a householder’s son, or one born into some other family, hears that Dhamma.
Having heard that Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata.
Endowed with that attainment of faith, he reflects thus:
"Household life is crowded and dusty; going forth is open air.
It is not easy, while dwelling in a home, to lead the holy life perfectly fulfilled, utterly pure, polished like a conch shell."
‘What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the household life into homelessness?
Then, at a later time, having abandoned a small or large mass of wealth,
and having abandoned a small or large circle of kinsmen, he shaves off his hair and beard.
Having clothed himself in saffron-colored robes, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness. Having thus gone forth,
he dwells restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfected in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults,
and training himself by undertaking the rules of training, through deeds of body and speech.
He is endowed with skillfulness, pure in livelihood, perfected in virtue, guarded in the doors of the senses, possessed of mindfulness and clear comprehension,
and contented. And how, young man, is a bhikkhu perfected in virtue?

In this case, student, a bhikkhu, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life; he lays aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, he dwells sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings.

That a bhikkhu, student, having abandoned the taking of life, abstains from taking life; that he lays aside the rod and the weapon, and being modest and compassionate, dwells sympathetic toward the welfare of all living beings—this, too, constitutes his virtue.
Or again, certain venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten food given in faith, maintain their lives by such low arts and wrong livelihood as these:
rites for propitiation, rites of prayer, rites for spirits, rites for the earth, rites for rain, rites for wind, rites for land, rites for clearing land,
rinsing the mouth, bathing, burnt offerings, emetics, purges, and upward purges.
He abstains from such wrong livelihood as the practice of low-caste arts, namely: administering purgatives, inducing vomiting, ear-oil, eye-salves,
nasal therapy, collyrium, counter-collyrium, surgery (sālākiya), extraction of foreign bodies (sallakattiya), the treatment of children, the provision of medicinal roots,
and the binding of medicinal herbs— such base sciences as these.
Furthermore, student, whatever way some venerable recluses and brahmins, having eaten meals given out of faith, make their living by such low arts and wrong livelihood as:
performing propitiatory rites, performing rites for the fulfillment of wishes... [and so on] ...the loosening of spells with herbs;
from such low arts and wrong livelihood he abstains.
This too belongs to his virtue.
A bhikkhu who is thus accomplished in virtue, young man, perceives no fear from any quarter, namely, regarding the restraint of virtue.
Just as a head-anointed kṣatriya king, having defeated his enemies, perceives no fear from any quarter, namely, regarding his adversaries; so it is with him.
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu who is thus perfected in virtue perceives no fear from any quarter, namely, regarding the restraint of virtue.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue, he experiences within himself the happiness of blamelessness.
It is in this way, young man, that a bhikkhu is perfected in virtue.
“This, young man, is that noble aggregate of virtue which the Blessed One praised, and in which he exhorted, settled, and established these people.
And there is indeed something further to be done.
“It is wonderful, Master Ānanda! It is marvelous, Master Ānanda!”
Thus, Master Ānanda, this noble aggregate of virtue is complete, not incomplete.
And such a complete noble aggregate of virtue, Master Ānanda, I do not see among other recluses and brahmins outside of here.
If other recluses and brahmins outside of here were to perceive within themselves such a complete noble aggregate of virtue, they would be satisfied with that alone:
‘This much is enough; this much has been done; we have attained the goal of recluseship; there is nothing further for us to do.
Yet, venerable Ānanda, you say:
‘There is indeed something further to be done here.’”

2. The Aggregate of Concentration “But what, Master Ānanda, is that noble aggregate of concentration which the venerable Gotama spoke in praise of, and in which he exhorted, settled, and established these people?
“And how, young man, is a bhikkhu guarded in the doors of the sense faculties?
In this case, student, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics.
Since, if he were to dwell with the faculty of the eye unrestrained, covetousness, dejection, and evil unwholesome states might flow in upon him,
he practices for its restraint, guards the faculty of the eye, and achieves restraint over the faculty of the eye.
Having heard a sound with the ear … having smelled an odor with the nose … having tasted a flavor with the tongue …
Having touched a tangible object with the body...
having cognized a mental phenomenon with the mind, one does not grasp at its signs nor grasp at its secondary characteristics;
for if one dwells with the faculty of the mind unrestrained, covetousness and dejection—evil, unwholesome states—might arise.
“...unwholesome states might flow in upon him; he practices for its restraint, guards the mind-faculty, and achieves restraint over the mind-faculty.
Possessed of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences within himself the untainted happiness.
It is in this way, young man, that a bhikkhu is one whose doors of the senses are guarded.”
And how, young man, is a bhikkhu endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension?
Here, young man, a bhikkhu acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside;
he acts with clear comprehension when bending and stretching his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension when wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl.
He acts with clear comprehension when eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in passing excrement and urine;
he acts with clear comprehension when going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
It is in this way, young man, that a bhikkhu is endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension.
And how, young man, is a bhikkhu contented?
Here, young man, a bhikkhu is contented with a robe for the body and almsfood for the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking only these with him.

Just as, young man, wherever a winged bird flies, it flies burdened only by its own wings; so too, a bhikkhu is contented with a robe for the body and almsfood for the belly. Wherever he goes, he goes taking only these with him.
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu is content with robes to protect the body and almsfood to sustain the belly. Wherever he goes, he sets out taking only these with him.
It is in this way, young man, that a bhikkhu is content.
Endowed with this noble aggregate of virtue and this noble restraint of the sense faculties...
Endowed with this noble mindfulness and clear comprehension, and endowed with this noble contentment, he resorts to a secluded lodging:
a forest, the foot of a tree, a mountain, a glen, a hillside cave, a charnel ground, a jungle thicket, an open space, or a heap of straw.
Having returned from his almsround after his meal, he sits down, folding his legs crosswise, setting his body erect, and establishing mindfulness before him.
Thus, having abandoned covetousness for the world, he dwells with a mind free from covetousness; he purifies his mind of covetousness.
Having abandoned ill will and hatred, he dwells with a mind free from ill will, compassionate and sympathetic toward all living beings; he purifies his mind of ill will and hatred.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, he dwells free from sloth and torpor, percipient of light, mindful and clearly comprehending; he purifies his mind of sloth and torpor.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, he dwells unagitated, with a mind calmed within; he purifies his mind of restlessness and remorse.
Having abandoned doubt, he dwells as one who has crossed beyond doubt, free from uncertainty regarding wholesome states; he purifies his mind of doubt.
It is just as if, young man, a man were to take a loan and apply himself to his work.
May those undertakings of his succeed.
He would clear away whatever old debts he had, and there might remain a surplus for the maintenance of his wife.
Then it would occur to him:
‘In the past, I indeed took a loan and engaged in work.
Those works of mine were successful.
Thus, I cleared away the principal of my former debts, and there remains a surplus for the maintenance of my wife.’
Thus, on that account, one might find joy and attain gladness.
Māṇava, it is just as if a man were afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill; he would have no appetite for food, and there would be no strength in his body.
After some time, he would be freed from that affliction, he would have an appetite for food, and there would be strength in his body.
It might occur to him:
"Formerly, I was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill; food did not agree with me, and there was no strength in my body.
But now I am freed from that affliction; food agrees with me, and there is strength in my body."
Thus, on that account, one would find joy and attain gladness.
It is just as if, young man, a man were bound in a prison,
and at a later time he were released from that prison in safety and security, with no loss of his wealth.
It would occur to him:
“Formerly, I was bound in prison.
Now I am released from that prison, safe and secure, and I have no loss of wealth whatsoever.”
Thus, on that account, one might find joy and attain gladness.
It is just as if, young man, a man were a slave—not his own master, dependent on others, and unable to go where he wishes.
At a later time, he might be released from that slavery; being his own master, no longer dependent on others, free, and able to go wherever he wishes.
It would occur to him:
"Formerly, I was a slave, not independent, dependent on others, and unable to go where I wished.
But now I am freed from that slavery; I am independent, no longer dependent on others, a free man, able to go wherever I wish."
On that account, one would find joy and attain happiness.
It is just as if, young man, a man with wealth and property were to set out on a long journey through a wilderness, a path where food is scarce and dangers abound.
After some time, he would cross over that wilderness and reach the edge of a village in safety—a place secure and free from danger.
It would occur to him:
"Formerly, I set out upon a long journey through a wilderness road that was destitute of food and full of danger;
but now I have crossed that wilderness, safely reached the vicinity of a village, and am established in safety, free from peril."
Thus, on that account, one might find joy and attain gladness.
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu regards these five hindrances as unabandoned within himself, just as one regards debt, disease, imprisonment, slavery, or a journey across a desert wilderness.
Young man, he regards them just as one regards freedom from debt, health, release from prison, the status of a free man, or a land of safety.
In the same way, bhikkhu, when these five hindrances have been abandoned in himself, he regards them as such.

As he regards these five hindrances as abandoned in himself, gladness arises; in one who is gladdened, rapture arises; for one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil; with a tranquil body, he experiences happiness; and for one who is happy, the mind becomes concentrated.

Thus, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and filled with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Thus he drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Just as, young man, a skilled bath-attendant or a bath-attendant’s apprentice, having poured bath-powder into a bronze basin, might knead it repeatedly with water until the ball of bath-powder becomes saturated with moisture—so too does he drench, steep, fill, and pervade this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion. There is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
It is filled with oil inside and out, saturated with oil, yet it does not leak.
In the same way, student, a bhikkhu drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion;
there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.

Furthermore, young man, when a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion;

he drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, so that there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
This, too, is his possession of concentration.

Furthermore, student, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal tranquility and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, and possesses the rapture and happiness born of concentration.

He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration; there is no part of his entire body that is not touched by the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
"Just as, young man, there might be a deep pool of water with its source bubbling up from within,
which has no inlet for water from the eastern direction, none from the southern direction, none from the western direction,
and none from the northern direction, and the rain does not fall at regular intervals..."
One might properly provide a stream of water at the right time. Yet, rather than that, a cool stream of water might well up from within that very pond itself,
drenching, suffusing, filling, and pervading that same pond with its cool water,
so that there would be no part of the entire pond not touched by that cool water.
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu...
[as before] ...when, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, he enters and dwells in the second jhāna...

He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the rapture and happiness born of concentration; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with the rapture and happiness born of concentration.
This too belongs to his concentration.
Furthermore, student, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending;
he experiences happiness with the body, of which the Noble Ones declare: “He who is equanimous and mindful dwells in happiness. This too belongs to his concentration.
He enters and dwells in the third jhāna.
He drenches, steeps, fills, and pervades this very body with a happiness devoid of rapture; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with happiness devoid of rapture.
Just as, young man, in a bed of blue lotuses, or pink lotuses, or white lotuses... some of the blue lotuses...
Or suppose there were blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses, born in the water, grown in the water, not emerging above the water, nourished while submerged;
from their tips down to their roots, they would be completely drenched, saturated, filled, and suffused with cool water,
such that there would be no part of those blue lotuses, red lotuses, or white lotuses untouched by the cool water.
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu...

[as before] ...furthermore, young man, with the fading away of rapture, a bhikkhu dwells having attained the third jhāna, which possesses equanimity and mindfulness and is described as "dwelling happily.
He drenches, steeps, fills, and suffuses this very body with the happiness divested of rapture; there is no part of his entire body that is not suffused with this happiness divested of rapture.
This, too, belongs to his concentration.
Furthermore, student, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief,
a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity.
Thus, having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and bright, he sits;
there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by the pure and bright mind.
Just as if, young man, a man were sitting having covered himself, including his head, with a white cloth, there would be no part of his entire body unpervaded by the white cloth.
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu...

[as before] ...and furthermore, young man, with the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, a bhikkhu enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
He sits having pervaded this very body with a mind that is pure and bright; there is no part of his entire body unpervaded by that pure and bright mind.
This too belongs to his concentration.
This, young man, is that noble aggregate of concentration which the Blessed One praised, and in which he exhorted, settled, and established these people.
And yet, there is still more to be done here.”
“It is wonderful, Master Ānanda! It is marvelous, Master Ānanda!
This noble aggregate of concentration, Master Ānanda, is complete and not incomplete.
And I do not see such a complete noble aggregate of concentration among the other ascetics and brahmins outside this teaching.”

"Master Ānanda, if other ascetics and brahmins outside this teaching were to perceive within themselves such a perfected noble aggregate of concentration, they would be satisfied with that alone, saying:
'Enough is done; enough has been achieved; we have attained the goal of asceticism; there is nothing further for us to do.
Yet Master Ānanda says this:"
‘And there is still more to be done here.
3. The Aggregate of Wisdom:
“But what, Master Ānanda, is that noble aggregate of wisdom of which Master Gotama was a speaker, in which he exhorted, settled, and established these people?”

“When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward knowledge and vision.
He understands thus:

‘This body of mine, possessed of form, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, fed on rice and gruel, is subject to impermanence, to being worn away, rubbed away, broken up, and destroyed; and this consciousness of mine is supported by it and bound up with it.’”
"And this consciousness of mine is dependent on this, bound to this.
It is just as if, young man, there were a beautiful beryl gem, of pure origin, eight-faceted, well-cut, clear, translucent, unclouded, and perfect in every aspect;
and into it a thread were strung—either blue, yellow, red, white, or pale yellow.
A man with good eyesight, taking it in his hand, would examine it thus:
"This is indeed a beautiful beryl gem, of noble birth, eight-faceted, well-polished, clear, translucent, unclouded, and perfect in every way.
And here is a thread woven through it—blue, or yellow, or red, or white, or pale yellow."
In the same way, young man, when a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated, pure, bright, unblemished, rid of defilement,
malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward knowledge and vision.
He understands thus:

‘This body of mine, indeed, is material, composed of the four great elements, born of mother and father, fed on rice and gruel, and is subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and massaged, to breaking apart and dissolution.
Yet this consciousness of mine is dependent upon it, bound to it.
When, young man, a bhikkhu’s mind is thus concentrated … [and so forth] …”
Having attained imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward knowledge and vision.
He understands thus:
“… [as before] … it is bound up herein.”
This too belongs to his wisdom.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the production of a mind-made body.
From this body he produces another body—material, mind-made, complete in all its limbs and faculties, and lacking no sense organ.
"Just as if, young man, a man were to pull a reed from its sheath, and it occurred to him:
'This is the sheath, this is the reed; the sheath is one thing, the reed is another; indeed, the reed has been pulled out from the sheath.'"
Or again, student, it is as if a man were to draw a sword from its scabbard.
It would occur to him:
"This is the sword; this is the scabbard. The sword is one thing, the scabbard another; the sword has indeed been drawn from the scabbard."
Or again, young man, suppose a man were to pull a snake out from its slough.
It would occur to him:
"This is the snake; this is the slough; the snake is one thing, the slough another; indeed, the snake has been drawn out from the slough."
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu...

[as before] ...Furthermore, young man, when the mind of a bhikkhu is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the production of a mind-made body... [as before] ...”
This too belongs to his wisdom.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the various powers of psychic transformation (*iddhividhā*).
He experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many; having been many, he becomes one...
He becomes one; he appears and disappears; he passes through walls, through enclosures, and through mountains without being obstructed, just as if through space;
he dives in and out of the earth as if it were water; he walks on water without breaking the surface as if on earth;
and he travels cross-legged through the sky like a winged bird.
He touches and strokes with his hand even these sun and moon, so powerful and majestic;
he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
Just as, young man, a skilled potter or a potter’s apprentice might fashion and produce whatever kind of vessel he desires from well-prepared clay.
Or again, young man, just as a skilled ivory-worker, or a pupil of a skilled ivory-worker, might fashion and produce whatever ivory article he desires from well-prepared ivory;
or just as a skilled goldsmith, or a pupil of a skilled goldsmith, might fashion and produce whatever golden article he desires from well-prepared gold.
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu— [as previously described]— when his mind is thus concentrated,
purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability,
directs and inclines it toward the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhā*).
Thus he experiences various kinds of psychic power: having been one, he becomes many …pe… he exercises mastery with his body as far as the Brahma-world.
This too is his wisdom.
With his mind thus concentrated …pe… having attained imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the divine ear-element.
Thus, with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, he hears both kinds of sounds—the divine and the human, whether far or near.
Just as, student, a man traveling along a highway might hear the sound of a kettle-drum, the sound of a drum, and the sound of a conch, a cymbal, and a gong;
and it would occur to him: "This is the sound of a kettle-drum," "This is the sound of a drum," and "This is the sound of a conch, a cymbal, and a gong."
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu...
[as before] ...and when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the divine ear-element.
With the divine ear-element, which is purified and surpasses the human, he hears both kinds of sounds: those of devas and those of humans, whether far or near.
This too is his wisdom.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, stainless, free from defilements, supple, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of the minds of others.
He understands the minds of other beings and other persons by encompassing them with his own mind.
He understands a mind with lust as "a mind with lust," he understands a mind without lust as "a mind without lust," and he understands a mind with hatred as "a mind with hatred."
He understands a mind free from hatred as ‘a mind free from hatred’;
he understands a deluded mind as ‘a deluded mind’;
or he understands a mind free from delusion as ‘a mind free from delusion.’
He understands a contracted mind as “a contracted mind,” he understands a distracted mind as “a distracted mind,” and he understands a magnified mind as “a magnified mind.”
He understands an unexalted mind as "an unexalted mind";
he understands an excelled mind as "an excelled mind";
or he understands an unsurpassed mind as "an unsurpassed mind."
He understands a concentrated mind as “a concentrated mind,” he understands an unconcentrated mind as “an unconcentrated mind,” and he understands a liberated mind as “a liberated mind.”
Or, when the mind is unliberated, he understands: ‘The mind is unliberated.

Just as, young man, a woman or a man—youthful, young, and fond of adornment—might examine his own facial reflection in a clear, bright, and polished mirror, or in a bowl of pure water, and [perceive] it with a blemish if there is a blemish.
He would know it as such; he would know a seedless one as seedless.

In the same way, student, a bhikkhu—[as previously described]—when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the penetration of others' minds.
Thus, having encompassed with his own mind the minds of other beings and other individuals, he understands them:
he understands a mind affected by lust as "a mind affected by lust" ...
[and so on] ... or he understands an unliberated mind as "an unliberated mind."
This too belongs to his wisdom.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, unblemished, free from impurities, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say: one birth, two births, three births... [and so on].
Whether four births, five births, ten births, twenty births, thirty births, forty births, fifty births,
a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, or many aeons of world-contraction,
many aeons of world-expansion, or many aeons of both world-contraction and expansion: "In that place I was..."
‘I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan.
Passing away from there, I was reborn elsewhere; there too I had such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan.
Passing away from there, I was reborn here. Thus he recollects his manifold past lives in their modes and their details.
He recollects his past lives.

It is just as if, young man, a man were to go from his own village to another village, and from that village to yet another village, and then from that village he were to return to his own village. He would think: "I..."
‘From my own village I went to that village; there I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and remained silent thus. From that village too I went to another village;
there also I stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and remained silent thus. Thus have I returned from that village back to my own village.’”

In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu... [as before] ...when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, cleansed, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of recollection of past lives.
He recollects his manifold past lives, that is to say, one birth... [as before] ...thus with their aspects and particulars he recollects his manifold past lives.
This, too, belongs to his wisdom.
Thus, with his mind thus concentrated ... having attained imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate; he understands how beings pass on according to their karma: "These [beings]..."
"Indeed, these venerable beings were possessed of misconduct in body, possessed of misconduct in speech, and possessed of misconduct in mind;
they were revilers of the noble ones, held wrong views, and undertook actions based on wrong views.
With the breakup of the body, after death, they have reappeared in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, even in hell. But as for these venerable ones..."
‘Beings who were endowed with good conduct of body, endowed with good conduct of speech, endowed with good conduct of mind,
who did not revile the noble ones, who held right view, and undertook kamma based on right view— these, with the breakup of the body, after death,
have been reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans...
He sees beings passing away and being reborn—lowly and exalted, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate;
he understands how beings fare according to their own karma.
It is just as if, young man, there were a palace at a crossroads, and a person with sight standing there were to look out.

Whether people were entering a house, leaving it, walking along a carriage road or a street, or sitting in the middle of a crossroads, he would think: "These people are entering the house; these are leaving;
these are walking along the carriage road or the street; these are sitting in the middle of the crossroads."
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu— [as before]—
when his mind is thus concentrated, purified, and attained to imperturbability, directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn— low and high, beautiful and ugly, fortunate and unfortunate— and he understands how beings fare according to their kamma.
This too belongs to his wisdom.

When his mind is thus concentrated, purified, bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs and inclines it toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of suffering."
He understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of suffering"; he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

He understands as it really is: "These are the taints"; he understands as it really is: "This is the origin of the taints"; he understands as it really is: "This is the cessation of the taints"; he understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints.
For one who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When liberated, the knowledge arises: "It is liberated.
One understands: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
Just as, young man, there might be a lake in a mountain cleft—clear, serene, and undisturbed. Therein...
A man with good eyesight standing on the bank might see oyster shells, gravel, and pebbles, as well as schools of fish, moving about or staying still.
He would think: "This pool of water is clear, serene, and undisturbed;
therein these oyster shells, gravel, and pebbles, as well as these schools of fish, are moving about or staying still."
In the same way, young man, a bhikkhu...

[as before] ...Furthermore, young man, when the mind of a bhikkhu is thus concentrated... [as before] ...having attained imperturbability, he directs and inclines his mind toward the knowledge of the destruction of the taints.
He understands, as it really is: "This is suffering"... [as before] ...
He understands as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of the taints.
For him who knows and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the taint of existence, and the mind is liberated from the taint of ignorance.
When liberated, there arises the knowledge: "It is liberated. "Birth is exhausted; the holy life has been lived..."
‘The holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
This too, young man, is his aggregate of wisdom. This, indeed, is that noble aggregate of wisdom which the Blessed One praised, in which he instructed the people, and wherein he established them.
"And there is nothing further to be done here.
"It is wonderful, Master Ānanda! It is marvelous, Master Ānanda!
This noble aggregate of wisdom, Master Ānanda, is fulfilled, not incomplete."
"Thus, Master Ānanda, I do not see this noble aggregate of wisdom so fulfilled among other recluses and brahmins outside of here;
indeed, there is nothing further to be done in this regard.
Excellent, Master Ānanda! Excellent, Master Ānanda!"
"Just as, Master Ānanda, one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost,
or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with sight might see forms— in the same way,
the Dhamma has been elucidated by Master Ānanda in many ways."
"Venerable Ānanda, I go for refuge to Master Gotama, and to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
May Master Ānanda accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.
The Subha Sutta, the tenth, is concluded.
